title: Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics
description: Jakob Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics for user interface design (1994). These heuristics are general principles for interaction design that help create more usable systems.
author: Jakob Nielsen

severity_scale.description: Nielsen Norman Group severity ratings for usability problems

0.label: No Problem
0.description: Not a usability problem at all

1.label: Cosmetic
1.description: Need not be fixed unless extra time is available on project

2.label: Minor
2.description: Fixing this should be given low priority

3.label: Major
3.description: Important to fix, should be given high priority

4.label: Catastrophic
4.description: Imperative to fix before product can be released

heuristics.name: Visibility of System Status
heuristics.short_description: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
heuristics.detailed_description: Users should never have to guess what the system is doing. The system should provide clear and immediate feedback about actions, system state, and progress. This reduces uncertainty and helps users feel in control.
key_principles: Provide feedback for every user action
Update status in real-time when possible

questions: Does the system provide feedback for every user action?
Is feedback provided within a reasonable timeframe (typically within 0.1 seconds for immediate feedback, 1 second for progress indicators)?
Are users informed about system status changes?
Do loading states clearly indicate progress?
Are users notified when background processes complete?
what_to_look_for: Visual confirmation of user actions (button states, highlights)
Status messages explaining what is happening

common_violations.example: User clicks 'Submit' but nothing indicates the form is processing
Page appears frozen without any loading indicator during data fetch
File upload shows no progress, leaving users uncertain about completion
Button doesn't change state immediately when clicked, causing users to click multiple times
Form submits but user receives no confirmation that action completed successfully

best_practices: Show loading spinners for operations taking more than 1 second
Use progress bars for operations with known duration
Provide immediate visual feedback (within 0.1 seconds) for clicks and interactions
Display success/error messages after operations complete
Show skeleton screens while content loads
Indicate system status in navigation/header (e.g., connection status)
Use subtle animations to indicate state transitions

quick_fixes: Add loading spinners to all async operations
Implement button disabled states during processing
Add toast notifications for action confirmations
comprehensive_solutions: Implement consistent feedback system across all interactions
Create progress indicators for multi-step processes
Add real-time status updates using websockets or polling
Implement optimistic UI updates with rollback on failure
Create a design system with standard feedback patterns
testing_approach: Test on slow connections to ensure feedback is visible
Verify feedback appears for all interactive elements
Check timing of feedback (immediate vs. delayed)
Test with users to confirm feedback is noticed and understood

heuristics.name: Match Between System and the Real World
heuristics.short_description: The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon. Follow real-world conventions, making information appear in a natural and logical order.
heuristics.detailed_description: Systems should communicate in language and concepts that users already understand from their real-world experience. This includes using familiar terminology, following real-world conventions, and presenting information in a natural, logical order that matches users' mental models.
key_principles: Present information in logical, natural order
Use culturally appropriate symbols and icons
Avoid technical jargon and system-oriented terms

questions: Does the interface use language familiar to the target audience?
Are metaphors and icons recognizable from real-world experience?
Is information organized in a way that matches users' mental models?
Are date formats, number formats, and conventions culturally appropriate?
Is technical jargon replaced with user-friendly terms?
what_to_look_for: Plain language instead of technical terms
Familiar metaphors (e.g., trash can for delete, folders for organization)
Natural ordering (e.g., first name before last name)
Industry-standard terminology for the user's domain

common_violations.example: Error message: 'API endpoint returned 500 status code' instead of 'Something went wrong, please try again'
Using abstract icons that don't represent their function clearly
Asking for password before username in a login form
Button labeled 'Instantiate Session' instead of 'Log In'
Using MM/DD/YYYY date format for international users who expect DD/MM/YYYY

best_practices: Use plain language and avoid technical terminology
Follow platform conventions (iOS, Android, Web standards)
Test terminology with actual users from target audience
Use universally recognized icons or pair icons with labels
Match the mental model of your specific user group
Localize not just language but cultural conventions
Order fields and information logically (chronological, alphabetical, or by frequency of use)
Use real-world metaphors consistently throughout the interface

quick_fixes: Replace technical terms with plain language alternatives
Add text labels to ambiguous icons
Reorder forms to match natural flow
comprehensive_solutions: Conduct user research to understand target audience's vocabulary
Create a content style guide based on user language
Implement localization for different regions and cultures
Design information architecture based on user mental models
Use card sorting to understand natural categorization
testing_approach: Conduct comprehension testing with target users
Test with users from different cultural backgrounds
Use A/B testing to compare terminology options
Analyze support tickets for terminology confusion

heuristics.name: User Control and Freedom
heuristics.short_description: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted action without having to go through an extended process.
heuristics.detailed_description: Users need to feel in control and be able to recover from mistakes easily. This means providing clear ways to undo actions, cancel operations, and exit from unwanted states. The system should support exploration without fear of irreversible consequences.
key_principles: Offer clear exit options from any state
Avoid forcing users down predetermined paths

questions: Can users easily undo their actions?
Are there clear ways to exit from modal dialogs, wizards, or processes?
Can users cancel ongoing operations?
Is it easy to go back to previous states?
Can users explore without fear of breaking things?
what_to_look_for: Ability to edit or delete created content
Ability to stop or cancel long-running operations

common_violations.issue: No way to undo destructive actions
common_violations.example: Delete button permanently removes data with no undo option
Modal popup has no close button or clicking outside doesn't dismiss it
Long-running process has no cancel button, forcing users to wait
Multi-step form only allows forward navigation, can't go back to fix errors
Form data is lost when user accidentally clicks back button

best_practices: Implement undo/redo for all significant actions
Provide clear 'Cancel' buttons in all dialogs and processes
Use soft deletes with recovery options (trash/recycle bin)
Add confirmation dialogs only for truly destructive actions
Save work automatically and preserve state
Allow navigation back and forth in multi-step processes
Enable ESC key to close modals and cancel actions
Show clear exit paths in navigation
Implement draft functionality for long forms

quick_fixes: Add undo option to destructive actions
Add visible close buttons to all modals
comprehensive_solutions: Implement system-wide undo/redo functionality
Create soft delete system with recovery period
Build draft/autosave system for all forms
Design multi-step processes with full bidirectional navigation
Implement session recovery for crashes
testing_approach: Test all destructive actions for undo capability
Verify all modals can be closed easily
Test form data preservation when navigating away
Check cancellation works for all long operations

heuristics.name: Consistency and Standards
heuristics.short_description: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.
heuristics.detailed_description: Consistency reduces cognitive load by ensuring users can apply knowledge from one part of your interface to another. Follow both internal consistency (within your product) and external consistency (platform conventions and industry standards).
key_principles: Maintain internal consistency throughout the product

questions: Are similar elements styled and behaving consistently?
Is terminology used consistently throughout?
Does the interface follow platform conventions?
Are actions placed in predictable locations?
Do similar actions produce similar results?
what_to_look_for: Standard placement of navigation and actions
Consistent use of colors for meanings (red for error, green for success)
Following platform patterns (hamburger menu, swipe gestures)

common_violations.example: Using 'Remove', 'Delete', and 'Discard' interchangeably for the same action

common_violations.issue: Varying button styles for similar actions
common_violations.example: Primary action button is blue on one page, green on another
Back button on left in some screens, right in others
Using non-standard gestures on mobile or unusual keyboard shortcuts
Some forms show errors inline, others only after submission

best_practices: Create and maintain a design system with reusable components
Document naming conventions and use them consistently
Follow platform guidelines (Material Design, Human Interface Guidelines)
Use standard icons and their conventional meanings
Maintain consistent layouts across similar pages
Apply uniform spacing, typography, and color usage
Keep navigation patterns consistent throughout
Use standard terminology from your industry
Position common elements (search, profile, settings) in expected locations

quick_fixes: Audit and standardize terminology across interface
comprehensive_solutions: Build comprehensive design system with components and guidelines
Create style guide documenting all patterns and conventions
Implement component library for consistent implementation
Conduct consistency audit across entire product
Establish design review process to maintain consistency
Create terminology dictionary for content creators
testing_approach: Conduct consistency audit across all screens
Test terminology usage with search
Compare against platform guidelines
Review similar features for pattern consistency

heuristics.name: Error Prevention
heuristics.short_description: Good error messages are important, but the best designs carefully prevent problems from occurring in the first place. Either eliminate error-prone conditions, or check for them and present users with a confirmation option before they commit to the action.
heuristics.detailed_description: Preventing errors is better than helping users recover from them. Design to eliminate error-prone conditions through constraints, defaults, and helpful suggestions. When errors are possible, warn users before they commit to potentially destructive or irreversible actions.
key_principles: Use constraints to prevent invalid input
Design to make errors difficult or impossible

questions: Does the interface constrain inputs to valid values?
Are there helpful defaults that prevent common mistakes?
Do users receive warnings before destructive actions?
Are error-prone situations identified and addressed?
Does the system help users make correct choices?
what_to_look_for: Disabled buttons/options when actions are invalid

common_violations.example: Form accepts invalid email addresses or phone numbers without checking
Delete button immediately removes data without asking for confirmation
Submit button can be clicked multiple times, creating duplicate orders
Calendar allows booking dates in the past
Quantity field defaults to 0, causing order errors

best_practices: Use appropriate input types (date pickers, number spinners)
Implement input masking for formatted data (phone, credit card)
Disable unavailable options rather than showing error after selection
Provide inline validation with immediate feedback
Use smart defaults based on user context and common choices
Require confirmation for destructive or irreversible actions
Implement duplicate submission prevention (disable button after click)
Show constraints clearly (password requirements, character limits)
Offer autocomplete and suggestions to guide correct input
Use progressive disclosure to avoid overwhelming users

quick_fixes: Add confirmation dialogs to delete actions
Disable submit button after first click
comprehensive_solutions: Implement comprehensive input validation framework
Build smart defaults system based on user behavior
Create confirmation pattern for all destructive actions
Implement constraint-based UI (disable invalid options)
Add autocomplete and suggestion systems
Build duplicate detection and prevention
Implement undo for actions instead of confirmation dialogs where possible
testing_approach: Test all input fields with invalid data
Verify confirmations appear for destructive actions
Test rapid clicking to catch duplicate submissions
Review analytics for common user errors to prevent them

heuristics.name: Recognition Rather Than Recall
heuristics.short_description: Minimize the user's memory load by making elements, actions, and options visible. The user should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another. Information required to use the design should be visible or easily retrievable when needed.
heuristics.detailed_description: Human memory is limited and unreliable. Design interfaces that show users what they need rather than requiring them to remember. Make options visible, provide context, and help users recognize information rather than having to recall it from memory.
key_principles: Use progressive disclosure to show relevant information

questions: Are all available options and actions visible?
Does the interface provide necessary context at each step?
Can users see their recent activity or history?
Are there reminders and hints where needed?
Do users have to remember information across screens?
what_to_look_for: Inline labels that persist when fields are filled

common_violations.example: Actions only accessible through memorized keyboard shortcuts with no visible menu
Form labels disappear when user starts typing, leaving no reference
Multi-step form doesn't show previous answers, requiring users to remember
Search field has no recent searches or suggestions, requiring users to retype
Deep navigation with no breadcrumbs or indication of where user is

best_practices: Keep form labels visible even when fields are filled
Show menus and toolbars rather than relying only on shortcuts
Provide autocomplete and search suggestions
Display recently used items and history
Use breadcrumbs for deep navigation hierarchies
Show previews before users commit to actions
Provide contextual help and tooltips
Display current state clearly (selected items, filters applied)
Use visual indicators for status (icons, colors, badges)
Keep related information together on the same screen

comprehensive_solutions: Implement persistent labels for all form fields
Build comprehensive search with history and suggestions
Create visible navigation showing current context
Add preview functionality before actions complete
Implement contextual help system
Build recently-used and frequently-used lists
Add visual indicators for all system states
Create summary screens showing selections before submission
testing_approach: Test workflows for required memorization
Verify all functionality is discoverable without documentation
Check that context is available at each step
Test with users new to the interface

heuristics.name: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
heuristics.short_description: Shortcuts — hidden from novice users — may speed up the interaction for the expert user so that the design can cater to both inexperienced and experienced users. Allow users to tailor frequent actions.
heuristics.detailed_description: Provide multiple ways to accomplish tasks to accommodate both novice and expert users. Accelerators like keyboard shortcuts, gestures, and customization options make experienced users more efficient without compromising usability for beginners.
key_principles: Support multiple ways to accomplish tasks

questions: Are there keyboard shortcuts for common actions?
Can users customize their workflow?
Are there quick actions for frequent tasks?
Can experienced users bypass intermediate steps?
Does the system remember user preferences?

common_violations.example: Application requires mouse for all actions, slowing down expert users
No way to pin or prioritize commonly used menu items
Users must delete items one at a time, no multi-select option
Users must set their preferences every session
Only one way to access a feature, forcing all users through same steps

best_practices: Implement standard keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Z, etc.)
Allow customization of workspace and frequently used features
Provide quick actions for common tasks
Enable batch/bulk operations where appropriate
Remember user preferences across sessions
Offer multiple ways to access features (menu, toolbar, shortcut, context menu)
Create templates or presets for repeated tasks
Implement smart suggestions based on user history
Allow drag-and-drop as alternative to menu actions
Support power-user features without cluttering novice interface

quick_fixes: Add keyboard shortcuts for top 10 actions
comprehensive_solutions: Implement comprehensive keyboard shortcut system
Build customizable dashboard and workspace
Create bulk operations for all applicable actions
Implement user preference system with sync
Build template and preset functionality
Add command palette for quick access to any action
Create macro recording for repeated workflows
Implement smart suggestions based on usage patterns
testing_approach: Test with expert users to identify needed shortcuts
Measure time-on-task for frequent operations
Test all actions for keyboard accessibility
Analyze usage patterns to identify customization opportunities

heuristics.name: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
heuristics.short_description: Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information in an interface competes with the relevant units of information and diminishes their relative visibility.
heuristics.detailed_description: Remove unnecessary elements and focus on essential content and functionality. Every element should serve a purpose. Extraneous information creates noise and reduces the prominence of important information. Good design is as little design as possible.
key_principles: Use progressive disclosure for advanced features

questions: Does every element serve a clear purpose?
Is the visual hierarchy clear and effective?
Are advanced features hidden until needed?
Is there unnecessary decoration or information?
Can users focus on their primary task?

common_violations.example: Screen shows all possible fields and options at once, overwhelming users
Heavy use of shadows, gradients, and effects that don't improve usability
Everything is same size/weight, no clear indication of importance
Every field has paragraph of explanatory text visible by default
Advanced settings mixed with basic options, cluttering interface

best_practices: Use progressive disclosure - show advanced features only when needed
Apply clear visual hierarchy with size, weight, and color
Remove decorative elements that don't serve functional purpose
Use whitespace effectively to create breathing room
Limit choices and options shown at once
Prioritize content - most important information should be most prominent
Simplify navigation - fewer menu items and levels
Use collapsible sections for secondary information
Keep text concise and scannable
Reduce visual noise (borders, dividers, shadows) to minimum necessary

quick_fixes: Hide advanced options in collapsible sections
comprehensive_solutions: Conduct information architecture review to eliminate redundancy
Implement progressive disclosure system for complexity
Redesign with clear visual hierarchy
Create simplified 'basic' mode with 'advanced' toggle
Audit all content for necessity and clarity
Implement card sorting to understand natural groupings
Remove or consolidate redundant features
Create focused task flows without distractions
testing_approach: Conduct heuristic evaluation focused on simplicity
Test information findability to ensure simplification didn't hide needed items
Measure task completion time before and after simplification
Get user feedback on clarity and focus

heuristics.name: Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
heuristics.short_description: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
heuristics.detailed_description: When errors occur, help users understand what went wrong and how to fix it. Error messages should be helpful, not blame the user, and should provide clear guidance for recovery. Good error handling turns frustrating moments into learning opportunities.
key_principles: Use plain language, not technical codes

questions: Are error messages written in plain language?
Do errors explain what went wrong?
Are solutions or next steps provided?
Are errors presented constructively?
Can users easily recover from errors?
what_to_look_for: Links or buttons to help fix the issue
Inline validation showing errors near their source
Clear visual distinction of error state

common_violations.example: Error: ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED (no explanation or guidance)
Something went wrong. Please try again.
Invalid email address (doesn't explain what makes it invalid)
You entered the wrong password instead of Password incorrect
Form shows all errors at top, user must hunt for which field has issue

best_practices: Write error messages in plain, non-technical language
Explain exactly what went wrong
Provide specific, actionable solutions
Show errors inline near the problematic field/element
Use appropriate visual indicators (color, icons) for errors
Avoid error codes or show them secondarily for support purposes
Use constructive language that doesn't blame the user
Link to relevant help documentation when appropriate
Offer automatic fixes when possible (e.g., 'Did you mean...?')
Make error states clearly distinguishable but not aggressive

quick_fixes: Rewrite error messages in plain language
Add specific solutions to error messages
Move errors inline near their source
comprehensive_solutions: Create error message library with consistent patterns
Implement inline validation for all forms
Build helpful error system with suggested actions
Add contextual help links to error messages
Implement smart suggestions (spell check, autocorrect)
Create error recovery workflows
Log errors for analysis to improve prevention
Design error states with clear visual indicators
testing_approach: Test all error scenarios to verify helpful messages
Have non-technical users read error messages for comprehension
Verify errors appear near their source
Test recovery paths from all error states
Analyze support tickets to improve common error messages

heuristics.name: Help and Documentation
heuristics.short_description: It's best if the system doesn't need any additional explanation. However, it may be necessary to provide documentation to help users understand how to complete their tasks.
heuristics.detailed_description: While interfaces should be self-explanatory, comprehensive help and documentation should be available when needed. Help should be easy to find, task-focused, concrete, and concise. Provide help in context where users need it.
key_principles: Make help easy to find and access
Focus on user tasks and goals

questions: Is help easily accessible when needed?
Is documentation organized by user tasks?
Are there concrete examples and steps?
Is help available in context?
Can users find answers quickly?

common_violations.example: Complex feature with no explanation or documentation
Help link buried in settings, not accessible from main interface
Help organized by technical features rather than user goals
Long help documentation with no search, forcing users to browse
Help text doesn't provide specific steps or examples for the task

best_practices: Provide contextual help (tooltips, inline hints) where users need it
Make help/support easily accessible from any screen
Organize documentation by user tasks and goals, not features
Include concrete examples and step-by-step instructions
Make documentation searchable
Use progressive onboarding for new users
Provide multiple help formats (tooltips, guides, videos)
Keep help content concise and scannable
Include visual aids (screenshots, diagrams, videos)
Maintain FAQ for common questions
Update documentation when features change

quick_fixes: Add visible help link to main navigation
comprehensive_solutions: Build comprehensive help center organized by user tasks
Implement contextual help system with inline assistance
Create interactive tutorials and onboarding
Add search functionality to documentation
Build knowledge base with examples and screenshots
Implement progressive disclosure in help (basic to advanced)
Create video tutorials for complex features
Add in-app guidance for new features
Implement chatbot or live support integration
testing_approach: Test help system with actual user questions
Verify help is findable from all relevant screens
Test search functionality for common queries
Analyze support tickets to identify missing documentation
Conduct usability testing on help content clarity

how_to_conduct_evaluation: 1. Review interface systematically against each heuristic
2. Document specific violations with screenshots and descriptions
3. Assign severity ratings (0-4) based on impact and frequency
6. Retest after fixes to verify improvements

severity_rating_guidance.frequency: How often does the problem occur?
severity_rating_guidance.impact: How difficult is it for users to overcome?

reporting_best_practices: Reference specific heuristic number and name
Explain why it's a problem (user impact)
